subject: science
title: US Middle School Science — Genetics and Heredity Reading
subtitle: Reading passages on DNA, inheritance, Punnett squares, environment, variation, and real-world genetics.
description: A reading pack that supports the genetics and heredity revision set. Passages focus on source concepts from the study pack, including DNA structure, inheritance models, data analysis, environmental effects, mutations, and applications of genetics.

data.sourcePassage: Genetics is the study of heredity, or how traits pass from parents to offspring. The instructions for many inherited traits are stored in DNA. DNA is a molecule found in most cells of living things. A gene is a section of DNA that helps control a trait or body process, often by giving instructions for making a protein. Proteins help build structures and control processes in cells. Because of this, genes can influence traits such as flower color, fur pattern, or disease resistance. A chromosome is a long, organized structure made of DNA and proteins. Humans usually have 46 chromosomes in most body cells, arranged in 23 pairs. One chromosome in each pair comes from the biological mother and one from the biological father. The connection can be summarized as DNA to gene to protein or cell process to trait.

data.sourcePassage: A Punnett square is a model used to predict possible allele combinations in offspring. In a simple pea plant example, T can represent a dominant tall allele and t can represent a recessive short allele. If two heterozygous parents, Tt and Tt, are crossed, each parent can pass on either T or t. The possible offspring genotypes are TT, Tt, Tt, and tt. This gives a genotype ratio of 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt. Because TT and Tt are tall in this simple model, the predicted phenotype ratio is 3 tall : 1 short. That means a 75% chance of tall offspring and a 25% chance of short offspring. A Punnett square shows probabilities, not guarantees. In a small group, the actual results may be close to the prediction but not exactly the same.

questions.question: Why might actual results differ from predicted Punnett-square percentages in a small group?
questions.modelAnswer: Probability does not guarantee exact results in small samples. Chance can make the actual numbers slightly different from predicted percentages.

questions.question: Why is Tt tall in this simple model?
questions.modelAnswer: Tt is tall because T is dominant, so one copy of the tall allele can show its effect in the phenotype.

data.sourcePassage: Traits can be influenced by genes, the environment, or both. In one investigation, students grew the same variety of bean plant in bright, medium, and low light for four weeks. Plants in bright light averaged 24 cm and had dark green leaves. Plants in medium light averaged 18 cm and had green leaves. Plants in low light averaged 9 cm and had pale green leaves. A reasonable claim is that light level affected plant growth. The evidence is the difference in average plant heights and leaf color observations. The reasoning is that plants use light energy for photosynthesis, which helps them make food needed for growth. Because the plants were the same variety, differences in light provide evidence that environment can affect phenotype.

data.sourcePassage: Variation means differences among individuals of the same species. Sexual reproduction usually creates more variation because offspring receive a mixture of alleles from two parents. Siblings from the same parents may inherit different combinations of alleles, which helps explain why they can share some traits but still look or act different. Asexual reproduction usually involves one parent and often produces offspring that are genetically identical or very similar, unless mutations occur. A mutation is a change in DNA. Mutations can happen when DNA is copied or when DNA is affected by environmental factors such as certain chemicals or radiation. Some mutations have no noticeable effect, some are harmful, and some can be helpful in certain environments. Variation matters because environments can change. A population with more variation may include individuals with traits that help them survive disease, climate shifts, or changes in food supply.

data.sourcePassage: Genetics is useful in agriculture, conservation, health, and forensic science. Farmers and scientists may use genetics to improve crops by selecting plants that grow well in dry conditions, resist disease, produce more food, or survive pests. Dog breeders have used selective breeding to choose dogs with desired traits, but focusing too strongly on a few traits can reduce genetic variation and increase inherited health problems. Conservation scientists use DNA to study endangered species, estimate genetic variation, identify related populations, and plan breeding programs. In health, family history can show increased risk for some conditions, but genes are not the only factor. Environment, nutrition, lifestyle, health care, and chance can matter too. Forensic scientists can compare DNA samples, but DNA evidence must be collected carefully to avoid contamination and should be considered with other evidence.
